text:
The first indication that the building lacked a waterproof membrane was not the rain, which had been entering for years, but an email describing it as “previously unanticipated water.”

Dr. Miriam Vale read the phrase twice. Outside her office, a man in a yellow vest lowered a swollen ceiling tile into a plastic sack.

“Was that supposed to be there?” she asked.

“Not anymore.”

Miriam chaired Comparative Literature, housed on the upper floors of Calder Hall, a building erected in 1978 and renovated whenever a donor’s name became available. The current donor’s portrait hung beside a screen displaying the university’s sustainability commitments.

At the emergency meeting, Simon Brice, director of estates, showed them a photograph of the roof.

“This,” he said, indicating a gray expanse, “is where the waterproofing layer would ordinarily be.”

“Where is it?” asked Celia Moss, who taught medieval literature.

“We have no evidence that it was installed.”

“Ever?” asked Peter Armitage.

“That is our current understanding.”

The omission had survived nine vice-chancellors, two mergers, and a campaign to rebrand the humanities as an innovation ecosystem. Miriam felt a brief, disloyal admiration.

The repairs would take twelve weeks.

***

For the first week, men looked at things. One photographed the stain above Miriam’s desk beside a ruler. Another photographed him photographing it.

Then drilling began above Celia’s seminar on devotional silence.

She continued for eleven minutes. As the students left, one said the noise had helped him understand the reading.

By Wednesday, the lift was blocked. The accessible entrance could be reached through a loading bay whose gates were sometimes locked. An email advised staff to “allow additional time for journeys within the building.”

“I used to go to the toilet,” Peter said. “Now I undertake a journey.”

Initially, people gathered in the kitchenette and exchanged photographs of dusty keyboards. Someone created a WhatsApp group called Membrane Theory.

Miriam posted a corridor sign:

DO NOT REMOVE THIS BUCKET  
THIS BUCKET IS IN USE

Underneath she wrote, *A distinction the department has struggled to maintain.*

It received seventeen laughing faces, including one from Noor Rahman, whose funding appeal Miriam had not answered.

Then the water was turned off without warning.

***

Noor shared a windowless room with four doctoral researchers and an air-conditioning unit declared nonfunctional, though it continued to make a noise.

She taught two seminars, worked Saturdays at the city library, and rented a room where cooking after nine was prohibited. The invitation to work from home had limited appeal.

“Where are we expected to go?” she asked.

“Alternative accommodation is being explored,” Miriam said.

“For us or the department?”

“For working.”

On Miriam’s screen was a spreadsheet of possible rooms. Most were booked. One was a laboratory. Another had, in the notes column, simply “piano.”

“I’m sorry,” Miriam said. “I don’t have a room yet.”

Noor nodded without looking angry.

That afternoon, the dean’s office offered six hot desks twenty minutes away.

“For thirty-two staff, plus researchers?” Miriam asked.

“Would a rota work?”

Miriam looked at the books, essays, and family photograph on her desk.

“I’ll ask.”

She did not ask.

***

The foreman, Danny, had a daughter applying to study English.

“What will she do with it?” he asked Miriam.

“She’ll find things she’s good at.”

“She’s already good at arguing.”

“Then she’ll have company.”

Danny did not control the schedule. First he said a task would finish on Friday. Then he said he had been told Friday. Finally, he began saying, “Let me find out what they’re saying now.”

There were separate contractors for roofing, ventilation, and temporary weather protection.

The temporary weather protection failed during an October storm.

Miriam found water cascading down the stairwell inside the plastic enclosure. Danny stood ankle-deep in it, on his phone.

“No,” he said. “Inside.”

He listened.

“Inside the building.”

***

By November, people were coughing.

This was not necessarily the building. There were children, crowded buses, a circulating virus. Nevertheless, dust settled overnight in the photocopier buttons and coated the kitchenette’s spider plant.

Noor’s childhood asthma returned. Each morning she wiped her desk and photographed the cloth.

Miriam forwarded the photographs to occupational health. The reply said there was “no established causal link at present.”

An air-quality consultant placed a machine in the corridor. During the test, the drilling stopped.

“Is this representative?” Miriam asked.

“Of?”

“Our normal conditions.”

He glanced at the silent ceiling.

“I measure what’s happening while I’m here.”

The report found acceptable particulate levels during sampling and recommended improved housekeeping.

“I’m dusting my books with a pastry brush,” Celia said. “What else do they want?”

The union advised documentation. Noor created a shared folder. Within two days it contained ninety-three files: blocked exits, damp patches, canceled classes, headaches.

Nothing immediately happened to the files.

***

“Why don’t you all refuse to go in?” Miriam’s husband asked over dinner.

“There are students.”

“There are patients when our sterilizer breaks. We still stop.”

“It isn’t quite the same.”

He waited.

She could have mentioned falling enrollment, vacant posts, the dean’s use of “footprint” while examining her budget. Empty offices might demonstrate that offices were unnecessary; canceled classes might demonstrate the same about staff.

Instead she said, “I know.”

“I’m not saying it’s your fault.”

“I know that, too.”

They ate quietly. He offered her the last peas. She accepted, although she did not want them.

***

The twelve weeks ended on Thursday. On Friday, a revised program arrived, its green bar extending into March. Beyond it lay a paler bar labeled “contingency,” with no visible end.

Everyone developed an arrangement.

Celia taught in the library, beyond reach of the café’s milk steamer. Peter arrived early and left before afternoon drilling. Noor borrowed a laboratory twice a week and learned not to touch anything.

Miriam kept trainers beneath her desk for the diverted route downstairs. On Fridays she took the office plant home, rinsed its leaves in the shower, and returned it on Monday.

Membrane Theory grew quieter. Captions shortened: *Fourth floor.* *Again.* *Does anyone know?*

At the winter reception, relocated to the business school, the dean thanked them for their resilience.

“We’re nearly through the worst,” he told Miriam.

“Are we?”

“That’s what estates tells me.”

Across the room, Noor was telling Celia about an interview in Glasgow. Miriam had written her reference the previous evening, praising her independence and contribution.

She had deleted “under difficult circumstances.” The building should not become part of Noor’s qualifications.

***

In February, the membrane arrived: enormous rolls wrapped in white plastic. Danny handed Miriam a sample, black and surprisingly thin.

“That’s it?”

“That’s it.”

She held it between finger and thumb. After so much correspondence, she had expected something more substantial.

Men unrolled it above the parapet. One wore a red hat; another paused to drink from a flask.

The smell resembled hot tyres. An email said it was not expected to present a significant hazard.

“Not significant to whom?” Celia asked, quietly, putting on her coat.

In March, the scaffolding came down. Daylight returned to Miriam’s office in sections. The stain was painted over; for two days, the white rectangle was the brightest thing there.

Noor got the Glasgow job. At her farewell, they gave her a book token and a mug showing Calder Hall.

“Before the works,” Peter said.

“Before we knew,” said Celia.

Later, Noor returned her key.

“Let me know how you get on,” Miriam said. “If you need anything.”

“I will.”

For a while, at least, Noor would need things from other people.

***

The final inspection was postponed twice. A drain needed attention. There was a question about flashing. The lift worked, stopped, then worked with a new noise estates said was normal.

In April, Miriam received a satisfaction survey.

She selected “neither satisfied nor dissatisfied” three times, then closed it without submitting.

Rain began that afternoon, steady and unremarkable. Beyond the uncovered windows, the gingko had opened its first leaves. A delivery driver leaned his bicycle against the courtyard sculpture.

Miriam watched the ceiling.

Nothing happened.

She returned to a dissertation proposal. After a paragraph, she looked up again.

Peter was telling someone he would definitely retire next year. Celia appeared to ask whether they could afford a replacement kettle.

“Order one,” Miriam said.

“A decent one?”

“Yes.”

When Celia left, Miriam moved papers back onto the shelf beneath the old stain. She had kept them away from that wall for months. Then she wiped the frame of her daughter’s photograph with her sleeve.

At five, the rain was still falling. In the corridor, an empty bucket stood beside the skirting board.

She considered carrying it to the cleaners’ cupboard, but did not know whether anyone still required it there.

She walked around it, switched off her light, and went downstairs.
